issues.body: `unwritten_integer_lexicals` enforces only `observed lexicals ⊆ written lexicals`; it does not prove that every still-live written term remains present. Meanwhile `normalize_term` maps distinct terms such as `"0105"^^xsd:integer` and `"+105"^^xsd:integer` to the same term. If the same subject/predicate/graph receives both spellings and sparq incorrectly drops or collapses one while retaining the other, Oxigraph also exposes one normalized quad, the normalized cross-compare passes, and the retained sparq lexical is in `written`, so the preservation oracle passes. The focused test proves current behavior on one fixed update but does not mutation-test this failure mode in the differential. Therefore the advertised strict lexical-preservation guarantee is not established.
issues.fix_hint: Track expected live sparq terms (including graph position and nested triple-term structure) through generated updates, or use a targeted per-operation oracle that verifies all inserted non-canonical term identities before an operation can legitimately remove them. Add a mutation/non-vacuity test constructing two same-value spellings at the same quad coordinates and a sparq snapshot missing one spelling; assert that the full adjudication path rejects it. Do not rely solely on the one-way unwritten-lexical set check.
issues.title: Numeric adjudication can hide loss of a distinct written RDF term

verdict.summary: The expanded differential harness has a soundness hole in its numeric-lexical adjudication. The retry projects distinct RDF terms onto the same canonical integer term, while the sparq-side oracle only rejects lexicals that were never generated. Together these checks can miss a sparq regression that collapses or drops one of two non-canonical spellings of the same value while retaining another written spelling. This contradicts the PR's claim that lexical preservation is pinned strictly.
